opening.headline: Let's explore why container serving costs are determined by compute pool configurations rather than service codes.
body: A service that serves a model via a REST API runs as an HTTP server on Snowpark Container Services. The location where the service is deployed is the compute pool, and credits are consumed proportionally to the number of nodes while the pool is running.

In this lesson, we examine in sequence the individual values of SQL used to create a pool, the behavior of automatic scaling and automatic termination, and service specifications that declare container resource requirements within the pool. We then explore how pool configurations impact cost and throughput through two illustrative examples.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: This explains the relationship between compute pools and service specifications.
The impact of full configuration on throughput and cost can be distinguished.

screens.title: Where are container serving costs determined?
screens.lead: First, let's examine the situation where costs are continuously increasing. Review the scene and think about where the costs are arising.

visual.alt: Service, compute pool, node structure arranged in three layers from top to bottom, along with a monthly credit consumption graph.
labels: Cost is accumulated on a per-node basis.

paragraphs: There is a service that serves a model via a REST API. The service code has not changed, yet the credits used for container serving increase monthly. In such cases, many people first try to optimize the code. However, the place where costs actually occur might not be the code itself.

Snowpark Container Services (SPCS) runs its services on a compute pool. A compute pool consists of one or more VM nodes, and credits are consumed in amounts equal to the number of nodes while the pool is active. Even if the service is lightweight, costs continue to accrue as long as nodes remain active in the pool.

Therefore, the full configuration sets the upper bound of cost. Whether to use a particular machine type, how many nodes to maintain at minimum and how many to scale up to maximum, and when to shut down during idle states are all part of the full configuration. The resource requirements for containers are defined by the service specification.
This lesson explains the relationship between compute pools and service specifications, and distinguishes how pool configurations affect throughput and cost.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Even if we modify the service code, how much can we reduce costs if the number of cluster nodes remains unchanged? Try to answer this question during the lecture.

screens.outro: Since we've verified the source of the cost, let's first consider how to determine the instance size.

screens.title: How do you determine the size of the compute pool?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Please first think about your answer mentally before clicking it.

items.prompt: When creating a virtual warehouse, recall how you selected the size from XSMALL to LARGE.
items.answer: Warehouse size is a value that balances the weight and cost of a workload. Similarly, the instance family of a compute pool has this characteristic. The document explains that determining a family is similar to determining warehouse size. The difference is that a pool includes a range of node counts rather than a single size.

items.prompt: If the usual request volume is significantly different from the sudden spike in requests, what value would be needed?
items.answer: When adjusting based only on normal conditions, performance degrades when load increases; when adjusting based on load conditions, waste occurs during normal operations. Therefore, the system receives a range defined by minimum and maximum node counts. Under normal conditions, it remains at the lower end, expanding upward when load increases.

items.prompt: What prevents a sudden surge in node count?
items.answer: The maximum number of nodes. The document explains that the maximum node limit prevents the automatic scaling process from adding more nodes than expected, acting as a cost ceiling during scenarios of sudden load spikes or code issues that cause a surge in requests.

screens.outro: Based on the question that comes to mind, let's go through the actual CREATE COMPUTE POOL command line by line.

screens.title: Building a Compute Pool: Family and Node Scope
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to step through the SQL statements line by line, with explanations showing what each line defines at each step.

steps.title: 1st line: Plant name
steps.body: `CREATE COMPUTE POOL summarizer_pool` sets the name of the pool. A compute pool is an account-level object, so its name must be unique within the account. Names containing special characters or case-sensitive quoted names are not supported.

steps.title: Row 2: Minimum node count
steps.body: `MIN_NODES = 1` is the lower bound for the number of nodes kept active. This value must be greater than zero. Setting a higher value allows you to use nodes immediately without waiting for automatic scaling during sudden load spikes, but it also incurs costs even under normal operating conditions.

steps.title: Row 3: Maximum number of nodes
steps.body: `MAX_NODES = 3` is the upper limit on the number of nodes that can be automatically scaled. Scaling is managed by Snowflake and will never exceed this value. Therefore, in the worst case scenario, the cost is determined by this value.

steps.title: Line 4: Instance family
steps.body: `INSTANCE_FAMILY = CPU_X64_XS` is the machine type of a node. The machine type determines the pool's resource capacity and the credits consumed by the pool during execution. Available families can be queried using `SHOW COMPUTE POOL INSTANCE FAMILIES`.

steps.title: Three required values
steps.body: Family, minimum node count, and maximum node count are essential values when creating a pool. These three values form the foundation of cost structure. A completed configuration creates a small pool with one to three nodes; other options serve to adjust costs over time. If any of these three values is missing, a pool cannot be created.

screens.outro: Having read the structure, I will now continue to examine how the node count changes over time.

screens.title: The cost curve generated by automatic scaling and automatic shutdown
screens.lead: Move the slider to sequentially compare the three full configurations. You can verify how the number of nodes and costs differ under the same request curve.

visual.alt: A stepped graph of node counts along a timeline, such as a demand curve over time.

stops.body: When creating a cluster, Snowflake first starts with the minimum number of nodes. Once the running nodes reach capacity and cannot accept any more, it adds nodes up to the maximum number of nodes. This setting maintains only one node under normal conditions and scales up to a maximum of three nodes during peak loads. This approach keeps costs low under normal operations and limits worst-case costs, but during surges, it requires waiting for the scaling process to complete.

If the minimum node count is set higher than 1, you can immediately use existing nodes instead of waiting for automatic scaling when a surge occurs. However, this results in consuming two node credits during normal operations. Nodes are removed if they remain inactive for a certain period, but the minimum node count is maintained.

The normal cost is the same as the first configuration, but if the load surges, the number of nodes can increase up to ten. While throughput increases, the worst-case cost ceiling rises significantly. Even in cases where request volume spikes due to client code errors, costs can accumulate up to the same ceiling, so the maximum number of nodes must be carefully set as a safety measure.

`AUTO_SUSPEND_SECS` stops the pool if no service runs for a period of this many seconds. The default value is 3600 seconds, and if set to 0, the pool will not automatically stop. `AUTO_RESUME` determines whether the pool is automatically awakened when a service request is made; if set to FALSE, the pool must be manually awakened via direct execution of `ALTER COMPUTE POOL`'s `RESUME`. If set to `INITIALLY_SUSPENDED = TRUE`, the node will not be launched at creation, preventing credit from being deducted.

screens.outro: If it's from the solution provider side, the resources required by the container are defined in the service specification.

screens.title: Service Specification: Resources used by containers on the full stack
screens.lead: Select each tab to examine a piece of the service specification YAML. Each piece explains what is defined and the symptoms that appear if it is misconfigured.

tabs.label: containers
tabs.body:
Service specifications are in YAML format and are provided together when creating a service. Containers are declared as follows.

```yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - name: summarizer
    image: <image path>
```

The `containers` field specifies which containers to run, and also allows configuration of `command`, `args`, and `env`.

tabs.label: resources
tabs.body:
Resource requirements are declared as `requests` and `limits`.

``yaml
resources:
  requests:
    memory: 4G
    cpu: 1
  limits:
    memory: 6G
    cpu: 2
```

``requests` represent the resources reserved on a node, while `limits` define the upper bounds that must not be exceeded. The number of containers that can fit on a node is determined by the `requests`, thus impacting the number of nodes required and consequently the cost.

tabs.label: endpoints
tabs.body:
The path called from outside is declared as `endpoints`.

`yaml
endpoints:
- name: api
  port: 8080
  public: true
``

`protocol is either TCP or HTTP. If the declared port differs from the port actually opened by the container, the call will not reach the container.

tabs.label: probe
tabs.body:
Check `readinessProbe` to confirm if readiness has been received.

```yaml
readinessProbe:
  port: 8080
  path: /health
```

Containers may remain in an unready state even if they are running if the path or port is misconfigured. Remember that service specifications refer to resource requirements, while the pool refers to resource provisioning.

screens.outro: Now I will explain two cases by using the complete configuration and specifications together.

screens.title: Explanation Example 1: The Same Service, Two Different Pool Configurations
screens.lead: The instructor compares two settings and provides an explanation. Select the right arrow to proceed step by step.

steps.title: Case conditions
steps.body: Assume you are the operator of this service. You serve an internal document summarization model via a REST API. Requests are steady during the day, but surge dramatically at month-end. You compare two different pool configurations for the same service.

steps.title: Setting A Analysis
steps.body: Setting A is `MIN_NODES=1`, `MAX_NODES=2`. Under normal conditions, only one node operates, keeping costs low, and the number can expand to at most two, thus keeping the upper limit of costs low. However, at month-end, when node availability is insufficient, response times may slow down.

steps.title: Setting B Analysis
steps.body: Setting B is `MIN_NODES=3`, `MAX_NODES=3`. Three nodes are always active, providing sufficient throughput and eliminating the need to wait for expansion. However, three node credits are deducted even during periods of low demand.

steps.title: Cost cap calculation
steps.body: The cost ceiling is determined by multiplying the maximum number of nodes by the consumption rate of the instance family. Thus, `MAX_NODES` serves as a safety mechanism. Both configurations have relatively low ceilings, but under normal conditions, setting B incurs three times the cost of setting A. Remember that throughput and cost are interrelated such that increasing one results in a corresponding increase in the other.

steps.title: Reading order
steps.body: When evaluating settings, you can sequentially ask three questions: how many nodes are typically running under normal conditions, how many nodes can increase during a surge, and when do they stop running in idle states. These three questions correspond to normal cost, worst-case cost, and waste time, respectively.

steps.title: conclusion
steps.body: Throughput is determined by the number of nodes and the family, while normal costs are influenced by the minimum number of nodes and downtime duration, and worst-case costs are driven by the maximum number of nodes. If the load pattern concentrates solely at month-end, consider adjusting the baseline to Setting A by slightly increasing the maximum node count or setting the minimum node count to 2. Regardless of the approach, it's essential to recognize that any increased upper limit directly translates to higher worst-case costs.

screens.outro: This time, I'll read and modify a configuration that has already seen a dramatic cost increase.

screens.title: Explanation Example 2: Reading and Correcting a Rampant Grass Setting
screens.lead: The instructor reads the pool settings from above for the credit appearing larger than expected on the end-of-month invoice. Use the right arrow to advance to the next step.

steps.title: setting of the problem
steps.body:
```sql
MIN_NODES = 1
MAX_NODES = 10
INSTANCE_FAMILY = CPU_X64_XS
AUTO_SUSPEND_SECS = 0
```
Read this setting line by line from top to bottom.

steps.title: Read 1: MAX_NODES = 10
steps.body: If client bugs cause request surges, nodes can scale up to ten. The cost ceiling is ten times the family consumption rate. There is essentially no mechanism to prevent surges.

steps.title: Read 2: AUTO_SUSPEND_SECS = 0
steps.body: 0 is the value that disables automatic termination. Even during idle periods, at least one node continues to run and does not shut down, so credits are still issued even during nights with no requests.

steps.title: Read 3: Specification requests
steps.body: If the `requests` specified in the service specification exceeds half of the node capacity, only one container can be deployed per node, leading to unnecessary node proliferation. Conversely, if it is too small compared to actual usage, multiple containers will concentrate on a single node, degrading performance.

steps.title: Revised version and compensation
steps.body: Set `MAX_NODES` to 3, a feasible value, change `AUTO_SUSPEND_SECS` to 600, the idle timeout period, and adjust `requests` to match actual usage. In return, response times may slow down during surges, and the first request may be delayed while a stopped pool restarts. Most cost-reduction measures come with such performance trade-offs and should be evaluated together.

steps.title: organizing
steps.body: In this case, the issue was not the service code but three lines of configuration. The pool sets the upper limit of supply, while the specification defines the size of demand. Only by aligning these two values can cost and throughput be balanced.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Summarizes the content covered in class. Read the paragraph below and proceed to the summary screen.

paragraphs: Container serving costs are determined by the compute pool, not by the service code. The pool consists of instance family, minimum and maximum node counts, and auto-termination and restart settings, which in turn influence throughput, baseline cost, and worst-case cost respectively.

The service specification declares the resources and endpoints required by the container, as well as the path to check readiness. The pool supplies those resources. If there is a misalignment between the two, symptoms such as increased cost or performance degradation may occur.
Finally, the most important safety mechanism is the maximum node count. It is a value designed to ensure that costs do not exceed the upper limit, even in the case of unexpected surges.

Let's go back to the first question. Even if you change the service code, if the number of pod nodes remains the same, costs will hardly decrease. To reduce costs, you must review the minimum node count, maximum node count, auto-termination time, and the requests specifications together.

glossary.def: A group of one or more VM nodes that run SPCS service and miscellaneous services. An account-level object created using CREATE COMPUTE POOL.
This specifies the machine type for a full node. It determines the node's resource capacity and credit consumption, similar to selecting a warehouse size.
This is the configuration provided together when declaring a service using YAML for container, endpoint, and resource requests.
This is the upper limit on the number of nodes that auto-scaling can add. A safety mechanism to limit costs during unexpected surges.
If the idle time in a pool exceeds this value, the pool is stopped. The default value is 3600 seconds, and if set to 0, the pool will not automatically stop.

misconceptions.myth: Optimizing service codes automatically reduces container costs.
misconceptions.fact: The cost occurs based on the pool family and the number of nodes. Even if the code is modified, if the pool configuration remains unchanged, the nodes will continue to remain online.

misconceptions.myth: The more MAX_NODES, the safer it is.
misconceptions.fact: When scaling occurs, nodes can continuously increase, leading to higher costs. The maximum number of nodes is a means to control costs.

misconceptions.myth: The resources in the service specification are independent of the total cost.
misconceptions.fact: The size of requests affects the number of containers that fit on a node, thereby influencing the total number of nodes required.

misconceptions.myth: Setting AUTO_SUSPEND_SECS to 0 will immediately turn off the device upon release.
misconceptions.fact: 0 is the value that disables automatic termination. Nodes remain active even during idle periods, resulting in continuous costs.

closing.lead: We will summarize the key points of today's class.
points: The full configuration sets the upper limit of cost.
A compute pool is composed of instance families, minimum and maximum node counts, and automatic stop-and-start settings.
Service specifications declare the resource requirements and endpoints of a container, and the cluster supplies those resources.
MAX_NODES is a safety mechanism that limits costs during a surge.
closing.reflectionLead: The following question is for your own reflection. Answers will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What is the maximum number of nodes in our tree, and what rationale was used to determine this value?

checks.q: In a compute pool created with a minimum of 1 node and a maximum of 4 nodes, if automatic shutdown is disabled and no service is running on any node, what happens to the nodes?
options: Idle nodes are removed, but at least the minimum number of nodes is maintained.
Nodes continue to increase until the number of nodes reaches the maximum node count.
All four nodes are maintained regardless of utility hours.
All nodes are immediately removed, including the minimum node count.
checks.explain: If a node fails to run services for a specified period of time, the node is removed, but the minimum number of nodes is maintained. The overall pool's suspension is separately defined by AUTO_SUSPEND_SECS.

wrong.1: Node addition occurs when the running nodes have reached their capacity and cannot accept any more. It does not happen during idle state.
wrong.2: Idle nodes are marked for removal, so the maximum number of nodes is not maintained as before.
wrong.3: The minimum node count persists even in idle state. Full shutdown is a separate action based on AUTO_SUSPEND_SECS.

checks.intro: We just learned the meaning of minimum and maximum nodes. Please verify how a idle node appears. This is an unrecorded self-check.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. Idle nodes are removed but the minimum number of nodes remains.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Sorry. The number of idle nodes is determined by the minimum node and removal rules.

checks.q: Pair the full configuration and service specification items with the target they define.
right: Number of nodes available at normal cost and instantly accessible during surge periods
Node machine type and consumed credit level
One container's usage of node resources
checks.explain: A family defines the node type and consumption rate, the maximum node sets the cost ceiling, and the minimum node specifies the normal cost and immediate throughput. The specifications' resources define the size required by the container.
checks.intro: Pair up the full configuration settings with their respective specification items. Scores are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: I have properly connected both pairs.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Some pairs do not match. Please reevaluate which item defines cost versus throughput.

checks.q: We have read the following pool configuration: MIN_NODES = 1, MAX_NODES = 10, INSTANCE_FAMILY = CPU_X64_XS, AUTO_SUSPEND_SECS = 0. If credits are still being charged even though there are no requests during nighttime, what is the most direct cause?
options: MAX_NODES is set to 10, so ten nodes are maintained even during nighttime.
The INSTANCE_FAMILY is XS and it continuously creates new nodes.
AUTO_SUSPEND_SECS = 0 disables auto suspend, and the release stops never resumes
When MIN_NODES is 1, the service is always executed twice.
checks.explain: If AUTO_SUSPEND_SECS is 0, Snowflake does not automatically suspend the cluster. Therefore, at least one node continues to run during idle periods, resulting in credit consumption.

wrong.0: MAX_NODES is an upper limit for scaling, not a requirement to maintain that many idle nodes. Idle nodes are removed, and only the minimum number of nodes remain.
wrong.1: The family determines the machine type and consumption rate of a node but does not repeatedly create nodes.
wrong.3: MIN_NODES is a lower bound on the number of nodes to be maintained and is unrelated to the number of service executions.

checks.intro: Review the settings to find the cause of continuous costs. An unrecorded self-audit.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. The most direct cause is that the automatic stop function is disabled, causing the release to not stop.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The cause is different. Please check again to confirm which setting controls the pause during idle time.
